Pharmacy Technician Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A pharmacy technician resume has to prove two things at once: that your fills are accurate and that you can keep up with the queue. Pharmacy managers do not hire on enthusiasm for medicine. They hire on accuracy rates, order volume, and the settings you can work in without supervision — and they check all three before they ever call you.

This guide gives you a full annotated example for a hospital pharmacy technician, the credentials hiring sides actually check, and the mistakes that quietly cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works for technicians: what you filled, at what volume, and with what accuracy.

Quick answer: A pharmacy technician resume should lead with dispensing accuracy, volume, and your CPhT credential and state registration; name PTCB and USP <797> training; and pair each experience bullet with a count, such as orders filled per day, waste cut, or inspections passed.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with accuracy and volume — 99.98%, 300+ orders a day, and the CPhT credential.
  • Prove safety and savings with waste figures, inspection findings, and wait times.
  • Name the settings and systems you work in: unit-dose, IV admixture, USP <797>, Pyxis, and Epic Willow.
  • Every bullet pairs a duty with a count: orders per day, waste cut, or inspections passed.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Pharmacy Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to a pharmacy manager or a director of pharmacy and you will not hear "passionate about helping people." You will hear:

  • Accuracy first. Your dispensing accuracy rate is the single number that matters most. "99.98% dispensing accuracy across quarterly audits" is a hiring signal; "responsible for accurate fills" is not.
  • Volume at pace. Orders filled per day, scripts per shift, IV preparations per week. Retail, hospital, and mail-order pharmacies all run at different volumes — name yours.
  • Sterile and IV work. Compounding, IV admixture, and clean-room practice separate hospital technicians from retail ones.
  • Inventory and waste control. Stock management, expiry tracking, and the dollars your ordering discipline saved — technicians who protected the budget get hired first.
  • Patient-facing calm. Insurance rejections, prior authorizations, and frustrated patients at the counter — hiring managers want technicians who resolve problems without escalating them.

If your resume reads like a course description — all training, no accuracy, no volume — it will lose to one that reads like a safety report.

Pharmacy Technician Resume Example

Below is a complete example for a hospital pharmacy technician with retail experience. It is fictional — the name and figures are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern real hiring managers respond to: what you filled, the volume, and the accuracy.

JAMES OKAFOR, CPhT
Houston, TX · (713) 555-0119 · james.okafor@email.com

SUMMARY
Certified Pharmacy Technician with 4 years filling orders in hospital and retail pharmacies, including 2 years on the inpatient team. Fill 300+ medication orders per day at 99.98% dispensing accuracy across quarterly audits, covering unit-dose distribution, IV admixture, and controlled-substance handling; cut medication waste by $18K a year through tighter expiry rotation. Certified Pharmacy Technician (PTCB); Texas state-registered.

CREDENTIALS
Certified Pharmacy Technician (CPhT) — PTCB, 2022 · Texas State Board of Pharmacy registration, current · Sterile compounding training (USP <797>) · HIPAA Privacy & Security training, current

SKILLS
Unit-dose distribution · IV admixture · Sterile compounding (USP <797>) · Controlled-substance handling · Pyxis & Omnicell dispensing systems · Medication reconciliation · Inventory management · Expiry rotation · Insurance adjudication · Prior authorizations · Pharmacy software (Epic Willow) · Patient counseling support

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Pharmacy Technician — Memorial City General Hospital, Houston, TX | 2023–Present - Fill 300+ inpatient medication orders per day at 99.98% dispensing accuracy on quarterly audits, covering unit-dose, IV admixture, and controlled substances - Prepare 60+ IV admixtures per week in the clean room under USP <797> standards, with zero contamination findings in the last two inspections - Cut medication waste by $18K a year by tightening expiry rotation and flagging slow-moving stock for return before it expired - Manage Pyxis dispensing stations across 4 nursing units, restocking daily and resolving discrepancies the same shift - Support pharmacists on medication reconciliation for 40+ admissions per week, catching duplicate therapies and allergy conflicts before the first dose

Pharmacy Technician — CVS Pharmacy, Houston, TX | 2021–2023 - Filled 200+ prescriptions per shift in a high-volume retail pharmacy at 99.9% accuracy, including data entry, counting, and final verification prep - Resolved 15+ insurance rejections per day by contacting prescribers and payers directly, keeping average patient wait time under 10 minutes - Ran the weekly inventory count and expiry sweep for a 2,000-item stockroom, cutting out-of-stock incidents by a quarter - Trained 4 new technicians on the dispensing workflow, insurance adjudication, and customer-service standards

EDUCATION
Pharmacy Technician Certificate — Houston Community College, 2021 High School Diploma — Westfield High School, Houston, TX, 2020

Why it works: the summary leads with the two numbers pharmacy managers check first — 99.98% accuracy and 300+ orders a day — then adds the credential. Every bullet pairs a task with a result: waste down, inspections clean, waits shorter.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: accuracy, volume, credential

"99.98% accuracy," "300+ orders per day," "CPhT" — three facts that let a pharmacy manager place you in thirty seconds. Lead with accuracy and volume, not with your training. If your accuracy rate is lower than you would like, lead with volume and setting coverage instead.

Experience: safety proof, not duties

Each bullet should answer "what changed because you filled it?" "Filled prescriptions" is a duty; "cut medication waste by $18K a year through tighter expiry rotation" is proof. Accuracy rate, orders per day, waste reduced, inspection findings, and wait times are the five metrics technicians are judged on — put at least three on your resume.

Credentials: put CPhT where buyers look

CPhT belongs in the header or summary, not buried at the bottom — it is the first filter for most technician roles. State registration matters too: most states require it, and hospitals check it before the interview. If you are exam-eligible but not yet certified, say so honestly ("CPhT exam scheduled") rather than implying the credential.

Settings: retail and hospital are different jobs

A retail technician's proof is scripts per shift, insurance rejections resolved, and wait times. A hospital technician's proof is IV admixtures, clean-room inspections, and unit-dose accuracy. If you have worked both, split the bullets by setting and let each role prove what that setting values.

Pharmacy Technician Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting's language exactly — "IV admixture" vs "compounding" matters to hospital filters:

  • Dispensing: unit-dose distribution, IV admixture, sterile compounding, USP <797>, controlled-substance handling, Pyxis, Omnicell, automated dispensing cabinets
  • Safety & quality: dispensing accuracy, medication reconciliation, allergy screening, duplicate-therapy checks, barcode verification, clean-room practice
  • Operations: inventory management, expiry rotation, stock ordering, waste reduction, insurance adjudication, prior authorizations, prescription data entry
  • Systems & people: Epic Willow, pharmacy management software, patient counseling support, prescriber communication, technician training

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Hospitals and pharmacy chains screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. Start from a clean template like the ones at Cvyon's template gallery, or the role page for pharmacy technicians. For the pharmacist side of the profession, see the pharmacist resume guide — a different role with different credentials.

5 Mistakes That Cost Pharmacy Technicians Interviews

  1. Duties without accuracy numbers. "Responsible for filling prescriptions" could describe any technician. Add your accuracy rate, your volume, or a result (waste cut, inspections passed, waits shortened) to every bullet.
  2. Hiding the credential. CPhT or state registration is the first thing a pharmacy manager looks for. If it sits at the bottom of page two, your resume may never reach a human. Put it in the header or summary.
  3. Claiming pharmacist scope you do not hold. Technicians do not verify prescriptions, counsel patients on therapy, or make clinical decisions. Claiming pharmacist duties you never held fails the first reference check and can end a candidacy outright.
  4. Vague compounding claims. "Experience with IVs" tells a hospital nothing. Name the setting, the volume, and the standard — "60+ IV admixtures per week in the clean room under USP <797>, zero contamination findings in two inspections."
  5. Listing every drug name you have handled. A wall of drug names reads as padding and dates fast. Name the systems and the settings instead — Pyxis, Epic Willow, unit-dose, sterile compounding.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a CPhT to become a pharmacy technician?

Most employers require it or expect you to earn it within your first year. The CPhT (from PTCB) is the credential most postings list first, and many states require registration or licensure on top of it. Retail chains sometimes hire uncertified technicians and train them, but hospital roles almost always require it up front.

How do I show accuracy if my employer never gave me a rate?

Use the closest honest proxy: audit results, inspection findings, waste figures, or the volume you sustained without rework. Never invent a percentage — a hiring manager can verify it, and a fabricated number ends the candidacy.

What is the difference between a pharmacy technician and a pharmacist?

Pharmacists verify prescriptions, counsel patients, and make clinical decisions; technicians fill, prepare, manage inventory, and handle the operational work under a pharmacist's supervision. The resume should make the boundary obvious.

Is retail or hospital pharmacy better for a technician?

Neither is better — they build different proof. Retail builds speed, insurance work, and patient-facing skill. Hospital builds IV and sterile compounding, unit-dose distribution, and clean-room discipline. If you want hospital work, get the sterile-compounding training and name it.

How long should a pharmacy technician resume be?

One page for most technicians, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a long career across genuinely different settings — retail, hospital, and mail-order — that each need space, and even then keep your accuracy and credential on page one.

Do I need a degree to become a pharmacy technician?

No. Most employers ask for a high-school diploma, state registration, and the CPhT credential from PTCB, rather than a degree. Certificate programs teach dispensing, compounding, and pharmacy law, and the exam proves you can work to the standard pharmacies audit against.
